title: Every outward ritual
hookLine: the Tenth Guru lists outward practices of many kinds and says all miss the secret without love (Savaiye)

lines: WHAT PEOPLE DO TO BE RELIGIOUS.
ALL AT ONCE, NEIGHBORS AND OWN.
cards: Make a list of everything people in one town do to be religious. Some wear something around their neck. Some keep a special object in the house.
Some face a certain direction to pray. Some walk to a holy place, some fast, some give to charity, some read the same book every day for years.
A poet looks at all of it at once, his own neighbors and his own people too, and asks one quiet question of every practice. Not is it right, or whose is best. Just: is the secret inside it?

teach.b: Two of the savaiye make long lists like this.

One, in paraphrase: bathing at pilgrim places, compassion, restraint, charity, vows and disciplines of many kinds; reading the scriptures of many peoples; living on air, keeping celibacy, weighing a thousand opinions.

Without the Lord, not one of these counts for anything. The other lists the outward signs of the Guru's world, things people carried, wore, faced and bowed to, the practices of the communities all around him.

teach.h: NO ONE FOUND THE SECRET, THE BHED.
teach.b: It ends: the whole world is tangled in false, outward rites, and no one has found the secret of the Lord. The word for secret is bhed, the hidden thing, what's actually going on inside. Hear it fairly.

teach.h: COMPASSION IS ON THE LIST TOO.
teach.b: The verse names practices of the Guru's neighbors, but it isn't a list of other people's mistakes. Compassion and charity are on it, things the Sikh Gurus taught constantly, so it can't mean they're bad.
It means they're empty when done for their own sake, as a box to tick.

teach.h: TURNED ON SIKH HABITS AS WELL.
teach.b: Sikh teachers are quick to turn it on Sikh habits too: bowing to the Guru Granth Sahib without listening to it, keeping the outward form while the heart is elsewhere, saying the Nitnem fast to get it done.
The secret, the savaiye have been saying all week, is love. A ritual with love in it is alive. The same ritual without it is a costume.

how: Many Sikhs recite these verses as part of the Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning, and gurdwara teachers often apply them to Sikh practice itself, warning against rituals done without love.

o: an outward rite done in the right order
the secret, the hidden heart of a thing
a holy object worn around the neck

games.q: every outward ritual — tap the pairs.

s: the savaiye's lists are about other religions' mistakes
compassion and charity are on the list, and Sikh teachers turn the verses on Sikh habits too.
one savaiya ends by saying no one has found the secret of the Lord
the world is tangled in false, outward rites; the hidden thing, the bhed, is missed.
the verses say compassion and charity are bad
they say even good practices are empty without the Lord, done only as a box to tick.

games.q: you've kept a religious habit for years, but lately you rush it to get it done. what would these savaiye ask you?
o: find the heart of it again: is love inside it?
do it twice as many times.
games.why: the savaiye don't say quit, or do more. they say every outward practice misses the secret without love. the fix is the heart, not the count.

practice: Pick one thing you do regularly, religious or not, a prayer, a visit, a call to a parent, a family dinner, and walk through it in your mind. Ask gently: is there love in it right now, or has it become a box I tick?
Don't judge the answer, just see it clearly, and if you pray, let Waheguru sit with it.

wordCard.voice: Bhed, the hidden thing. The savaiye's long lists of practices, and the line that says the whole world is tangled in them and hasn't found the secret.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bhed, the secret or hidden thing; the verse says the world tangled in rituals hasn't found the Lord's.

carryVoice: Your line: the secret is love. The heart, not the count. Day three hundred sixty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Akal Ustat, Tav Prasad Savaiye (the savaiya 'teerath nhaan daiaa dam daan')
Akal Ustat 30 (Tav Prasad Savaiye, the savaiya 'kaahoo lai paahan pooj dhario sir', ending 'bhed na paaio')
